summary: Dipyridamole is an antiplatelet and coronary vasodilator indicated, in oral tablet form, as an adjunct to coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin) for the prevention of postoperative thromboembolic complications of cardiac valve replacement. It increases platelet and tissue adenosine and cAMP, inhibiting platelet aggregation. Common effects are dizziness, headache, and GI upset, usually mild and transient. Because it is a vasodilator, it should be used cautiously in hypotension and unstable angina. Aspirin is not given concomitantly with coumarin anticoagulants in this setting.
indications: Adjunct to coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin) in the prevention of postoperative thromboembolic complications of cardiac valve replacement

dosage.c: Thromboembolism prophylaxis after cardiac valve replacement
dosage.d: 75 to 100 mg four times daily as an adjunct to usual warfarin therapy
dosage.n: Aspirin is not to be given concomitantly with coumarin anticoagulants in this regimen

admin: Take orally, ideally on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) for best absorption
May take with food to reduce gastric upset
Continue concurrent warfarin and maintain target INR as directed
Do not start aspirin concurrently with coumarin therapy in this indication
The intravenous form (for cardiac stress imaging) is a separate product given only in monitored settings
moa: Dipyridamole inhibits the cellular uptake of adenosine into platelets, endothelial cells, and erythrocytes, increasing local adenosine concentrations that act on the platelet A2 receptor to stimulate adenylate cyclase and raise platelet cyclic AMP. It also inhibits phosphodiesterase, further increasing cyclic AMP/GMP. The net effect is inhibition of platelet aggregation in response to stimuli such as platelet-activating factor, collagen, and ADP. The rise in adenosine also produces coronary and systemic vasodilation.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to dipyridamole or any component of the formulation
relative: Unstable angina or recent myocardial infarction (vasodilation may provoke ischemia, especially with IV use)

preg: There are limited data in pregnant women. Animal studies have not shown harm at therapeutic doses; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: Dipyridamole is excreted in human milk. Exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman; consider benefit to the mother versus potential risk to the infant.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established. Use with caution in renal impairment and monitor for accumulation of effects.
hepatic: Dipyridamole is metabolized in the liver and excreted predominantly in the bile. Use with caution in hepatic impairment; elevated liver enzymes and (rarely) hepatic failure have been reported.

major: Adenosine and regadenoson - dipyridamole increases their plasma levels and cardiovascular effects; adjust adenosine dose and avoid use before pharmacologic stress testing per protocol
moderate: Anticoagulants (warfarin) and other antiplatelet agents - increased bleeding risk (used together intentionally here, monitor)
Cholinesterase inhibitors - dipyridamole may counteract their effect, worsening myasthenia gravis
interactions.food: Best absorbed on an empty stomach; food can reduce/delay absorption.
interactions.alcohol: May add to dizziness and hypotension; limit intake.
interactions.diagnostics: Used intravenously as a pharmacologic stressor in myocardial perfusion imaging; can rarely raise liver enzymes.

rare: Cholelithiasis (with chronic use, due to biliary excretion)
emergency: Myocardial infarction / acute coronary ischemia (notably with IV use)

monitoring: Blood pressure and symptoms of hypotension
Cardiac symptoms (chest pain) especially during IV stress testing
Liver function if hepatic dysfunction suspected
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed, usually four times a day, ideally on an empty stomach
Continue your blood thinner (warfarin) and attend INR blood tests
Dizziness, headache, and stomach upset are common at first and usually settle
Stand up slowly to avoid lightheadedness
Report chest pain, fainting, or unusual bleeding to your doctor
pk: Antiplatelet effect within ~1-2 hours of an oral dose
Peak plasma concentration about 75 minutes after an oral dose
Dosed four times daily to maintain effect
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture
pearls: Approved oral indication is narrow - adjunct to warfarin after cardiac valve replacement
Potentiates adenosine and regadenoson - hold before pharmacologic stress tests and adjust dosing
Vasodilator: can cause hypotension and may provoke angina, especially intravenously
Often combined with aspirin (extended-release dipyridamole/aspirin) for secondary stroke prevention - a different product
Eliminated via bile; chronic use can rarely contribute to gallstones
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not double up. Try to space doses evenly across the day.
overdose: Overdose may cause hypotension, flushing, warmth, sweating, restlessness, weakness, dizziness, and tachycardia. Treatment is symptomatic; because of extensive tissue distribution and biliary elimination, dialysis is unlikely to help. Intravenous aminophylline can reverse hemodynamic effects of IV dipyridamole used in stress testing; vasopressors may be needed for severe hypotension.
